title: A pile of coins
prompt:
A pile of coins is counted out in different ways: in groups of 4, 3 coins are left over; in groups of 6, 5 coins are left over; in groups of 9, 8 coins are left over. There is at least one coin.

What is the smallest number of coins the pile could hold?
hints: In each way of counting, how many more would you need to make the last group complete?
What does that tell you about the pile if you imagine adding that many?
What is the smallest positive number that every group size divides exactly?
solution:
**35.**

Every group size leaves the pile 1 short of a full group. So if 1 more coin were added, every group size would divide the pile exactly. The pile plus 1 would be a common multiple of 4, 6, 9.

The smallest common multiple is lcm(4, 6, 9) = 36, so the pile is 36 − 1 = **35**.

The common slip is multiplying the group sizes, which gives 216, instead of taking the least common multiple, 36.
